title: State Best Practices
description: Learn patterns and best practices for managing state effectively.

data.text: Good state management makes apps predictable and easy to debug. This lesson teaches you where to put state, when to lift it up, how to group related values, and when to avoid storing derived data.
Keep State as Local as Possible
Only keep state in a component if no other component needs that data. Local state reduces re-renders and makes components self-contained and reusable.

data.title: Local vs Shared State

data.text: When multiple components need the same changing data, move it to their closest common parent. This is called **lifting state up**.

data.title: Lifting State Up

data.text: If two state values always change together, group them into a single object. This keeps related data synchronized and reduces the chance of inconsistent UI.

data.title: Grouped State
data.content: Combining related values into one state object

data.text: Do not store values in state that can be calculated from other state or props during render. Duplicating data creates a second source of truth and invites bugs.

data.title: Derived Values
data.content: Calculating values instead of duplicating them in state

data.text: Each piece of data should have exactly one owner. If two components need the same value, lift it to their nearest common ancestor or use Context.

data.caption: Lifting state up to the nearest common parent.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Parent] -->|prop| B[Child 1]

terms.definition: Moving state to a common parent so multiple children can share it.
A value computed from props or other state; should not be duplicated in state.
Each piece of data lives in exactly one place.

data.title: Exercise: Refactor a Temperature Converter
data.description: Identify derived state and lift shared state to the parent.
steps: Create a TemperatureConverter with Celsius and Fahrenheit inputs.
Initially, put state in each input separately.
Notice the inputs get out of sync.
Lift the temperature state to the parent and pass it down.
Verify both inputs now stay in sync.
data.expectedOutcome: A converter where both inputs reflect the same temperature because they share a single state owner.

items.question: When should I use Context instead of lifting state up?
items.answer: Use Context when prop drilling through 3+ levels becomes painful. For sibling communication, lifting state up is simpler and more explicit.

items.question: Should every piece of state be at the top level?
items.answer: No. Keep state as low as possible. Only lift it when multiple components genuinely need the same live data.

items.question: Is useEffect required for derived values?
items.answer: No. Calculate derived values during render. useEffect adds complexity and can cause stale closures.

items.question: What if my state object becomes too large?
items.answer: Consider splitting it into multiple useState calls, using useReducer, or normalizing the shape with an ID map.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Keep state local unless multiple components need it.
Lift shared state to the nearest common parent.
Group values that always change together.
Never store derived values in state — calculate them during render.
Maintain a single source of truth for every piece of data.
data.takeaway: Good state architecture prevents bugs before they happen. Next, you'll apply these patterns to forms with controlled components.
